summaries.summary: Deep learning excels in speech tasks, but robust training needs powerful GPUs and standard large-scale datasets, with text-independent speaker verification supported by NIST SRE evaluations and VoxCeleb.
Text-dependent speaker recognition lacks large-scale public databases, with RSR2015 containing 300 individuals and RedDots only 64 speakers, motivating DeepMine collection as a standard benchmark.
ASR systems need large, variable training data, available for English, Mandarin, and French but not Persian, motivating collection of a large-scale dataset for robust Persian ASR models.
The DeepMine project aimed to collect speech from at least a few thousand speakers, began in 2017, finished at the end of 2018, and released its cleaned-up database at the beginning of 2019.
DeepMine is publicly available under varied licenses, was crowdsourced using an Android application where respondents recorded phrases across sessions with utterance checks.
Database cleanup filtered problematic utterances using an alignment stage similar to LibriSpeech, with custom decoding graphs allowing word skipping and insertion for each phrase.

Erroneous utterances were removed from text-dependent and text-prompted lists, while correctly aligned sub-parts were kept for speech recognition, leaving around 190 thousand full-transcription and 10 thousand sub-part utterances.
After processing, 1969 respondents remained, including 1149 male and 820 female, with 297 unable to read English and about 13200 female sessions versus about 9500 male sessions.
The database website provides its latest status, availability information, and a limited number of samples.

DeepMine has three parts for text-dependent speaker verification, text-prompted speaker verification, and text-independent speaker verification or Persian ASR, with English text-dependent phrases selected from part1 of RedDots.
“My voice is my password.”
“OK Google.”
“Artificial intelligence is for real.”
“Actions speak louder than words.”
“There is no such thing as a free lunch.”
Part1 contains fixed phrases for text-dependent verification, with each speaker uttering 5 Persian phrases and, if able to read English, 5 phrases from Part1 of RedDots.
Three experimental setups use speakers with more recording sessions for evaluation and the rest for background training, with fewer English speakers and a small “dev” set in each setup.
Official trial lists vary enrollment utterances from 3 to 6 with one test utterance, and the 100-spk with 3-session enrollment (3-sess) is the main evaluation condition.
Part2 presents 3 random Persian month-name sequences per session in enrollment and test modes, with English digit sequences also recorded for respondents who can read English.
Three text-prompted setups define trials with 1- to 3-sess enrollment, seq or full test utterances, and the 100-spk with 1-session enrolment (1-sess) as the main evaluation condition.

Part3 displays 8 Persian phrases with phone-level transcriptions, mostly from news and Persian Wikipedia, and prompts 8 additional Persian phrases for respondents unable to read English to reach exactly 24 phrases per session.
Part3 can support text-independent speaker verification, text-prompted speaker verification using random text, and large vocabulary speech recognition in Persian.
Two speaker verification setups assign respondents with at least 17 or at least 8 sessions to evaluation, respondents with 16 or 6 or 7 sessions to development, and the rest to background.
Text-independent SV considers 4 enrollment scenarios and 4 test scenarios, with 1sess-1utt and 1sess-1sess for the 438-spk set as main evaluation setups.
Text-prompted SV with random text can use the same setup as the text-independent case together with corresponding utterance transcriptions.
Part3 supports Persian read speech recognition and speaker recognition applications such as training DNNs for bottleneck features or collecting sufficient statistics for i-vector training.
The ASR setup randomly selected 50 speakers, with test-set, large-test-set and train-set containing 5.9, 28.5 and 450 hours of speech respectively.
About 8300 Part3 utterances contain only Persian full names, with phoneme transcriptions extracted automatically using a trained Grapheme-to-Phoneme (G2P), for evaluating name recognition.
Due to space limitation, results are presented only for Persian text-dependent speaker verification and speech recognition.
A text-dependent speaker verification experiment applied an i-vector method to the Persian portion of Part1, using 20-dimensional MFCC features with derivatives from 16 kHz signals via HTK.
The reported system uses 400-dimensional gender independent i-vectors, length normalization, RWCCN, cosine distance, s-norm, and monophone HMMs with 3 states and 8 Gaussian components.
Speaker verification results use EER, $\mathrm {NDCF_{0.01}^{min}}$, and $\mathrm {NDCF_{0.001}^{min}}$, with only correct trials considered for evaluating systems.
Table TABREF23 reports Persian 100-spk and 3-sess results filtered by respondents' mobile brand and model, with “NN” target trials and “YY” non-target trials most difficult.
DeepMine is more challenging than RSR2015 and RedDots, with EERs without channel-compensation techniques of 2.1 and 3.7% for males and females respectively.
DeepMine includes target speakers with more than one mobile device, enabling analysis of channel compensation, with severe degradation for difficult device-model trials, especially females.
The third row shows the condition where target speakers use exactly the same device at test time as enrollment, demonstrating improvement over the first row.
The fourth row shows imposter speakers using the same device model at test time, with no device mismatch and degradation compared with the third row.
The fifth row shows negligible degradation when imposter speakers use the same brand but a different model, indicating different recording channel properties within a brand.
The sixth row shows degraded female results from using a different device model from the same brand for target trials, while male filters yield very similar results.
Female trials perform significantly worse than males in rows with possible device mismatch, while rows 3 to 6 show comparable performance, suggesting problematic device-mismatch trials.
The last row relaxes the second-row condition, requiring different target device models possibly from the same brand and imposter devices only from the same brand, yielding smaller degradation.
Speech recognition experiments on Part3 used Kaldi, 20 thousands shortest utterances for HMM-based MonoPhone, whole training data otherwise, a 16-layer F-TDNN, LF-MMI, and a 90,000-word dictionary.
Table TABREF26 reports word error rate (WER) results showing the database can train well performing and practically usable Persian ASR models.

The final DeepMine database is a crowdsourced large speech corpus claimed as the largest public text-dependent and text-prompted speaker verification database in Persian and English, with phone-level transcription.
Evaluation protocols for each database part study channels, duration and phrase text, and two speech recognition test sets include a normal set and a large set with 30 minutes on average.
Baseline results include i-vector/HMM on Persian text-dependent part and Kaldi speech recognition experiments, with DeepMine more challenging than RSR2015 and RedDots databases.
Sharif DeepMine company mainly supported data collection, while GACR project "NEUREM3" No. 19-26934X and NPU II project "IT4Innovations excellence in science - LQ1602" supported the paper.
